newsitem.title: USA: GM sees continued N. American profit gains.
newsitem.headline: GM sees continued N. American profit gains.

text.p: General Motors Corp Chief Financial Officer J. Michael Losh said he expects the automaker's North American vehicle operations to continue to post year-over-year earnings improvments.
Losh also told reporters on a conference call that GM's European operations are likely to post quarterly profits for the remainder of 1997 and should be in the black for the full year.
"As we go through the year, I expect NAO to improve their market share, particularly in the second half of the year and i expect them to continue to have year-to-year profit improvements," Losh said.

GM's North American Operations, which now consist of its vehicle assembly, powertrain and stamping operations, posted a net profit of $764 million in the first quarter, versus a year-earlier loss of $279 million, which included a $750 million negative impact from a 17-day brake plant strike in March 1996.

Although GM's U.S. retail incentives increased to $860 from $598, Losh said the increase was not attributable to the many new car models GM has recently introduced. Rather, the incentives were increased on existing car and truck models and those being replaced by new vehicles.

GM-Europe posted first quarter operating earnings of $94 million, down sharply from a year-earlier profit of $285 million. The first quarter 1997 results excluded a $55 million gain from the settlement of GM's industrial espionage dispute with Volkswagen AG.
"In general I expect Europe to stay in the black," Losh said. "They were black in the first quarter and I expect them to be black for the balance of the year."

Losh said he was encouraged that some other automakers in Europe are taking actions to eliminate excess capacity and cited Renault SA's decision to close its Vilvoorde, Belgium plant. He said GM's European capacity is currently in line with demand.

Losh said GM is about two-thirds of the way finished with its current plans to buy back $2.5 billion worth of common stock, which were announced in January. Although he did not offer a timetable for completion of the program, he said GM expects to "move briskly" on it.
The auto giant spent about $1.6 billion during the first quarter to buy back about $27 million shares of its $1-2/3 par-value stock, also known as its parent-company stock.
